title: India to Release AI Regulation Consultation Paper Within a Month, Vaishnaw Says
excerpt: IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw announced the consultation paper will cover AI safety, deepfakes, and the technology's psychological impact — with industry expected to carry the main burden of compliance.
body:
• IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said the government will release a consultation paper on AI regulation within a month, laying out India's approach to AI safety, human-centric use, skilling, and inclusive growth.
  • Deepfakes are a central focus: the paper will examine the risks of false or misleading AI-generated content and the measures that could mitigate that harm.
  • The consultation will also study the possible psychological effects of AI, and Vaishnaw said industry will carry the main burden of managing AI-related risks: "The bulk of the responsibility has to be on industry."
  • What it means for users and platforms: this paper precedes future rules. Under the amended IT Rules already notified this year, platforms must label synthetic content and can face a 3-hour takedown window for non-consensual deepfakes — the consultation will shape what comes next. This is distinct from Prime Minister Modi's call for a global anti-fraud framework made separately at the India Mobile Congress.

India will release a consultation paper on artificial intelligence regulation within a month, Union IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said, marking the first concrete step toward a formal regulatory framework for AI in the country.

Speaking at an event, Vaishnaw said the paper will lay out how the government approaches AI safety, keeping humans at the center of development and use, and ensuring AI-led change remains inclusive, "with no section of society being left behind." Industry stakeholders will be asked for detailed feedback before the government finalizes its regulatory approach.

"The bulk of the responsibility has to be on industry."

— Ashwini Vaishnaw, Union Minister for Electronics and Information Technology

Deepfakes and the psychology of AI in focus

Two areas will get particular attention. Vaishnaw said the quality of deepfakes is improving every day, raising the risk that people will be misled or manipulated by them, and the consultation will examine the dangers of false or misleading AI-generated content along with possible countermeasures.

The paper will also study the potential psychological impact of AI — including its role in some psychological disorders — as AI assistants and companion tools become part of everyday life and raise new questions about their effect on individuals and society. Skilling and inclusion round out the agenda: the government wants a framework that helps workers adapt rather than leaving them behind.

From rules to a full AI law

The consultation paper arrives as India is already tightening the screws on synthetic content through the amended IT Rules. The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology notified amendments to the IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 earlier this year that target "synthetically generated information": platforms must ensure AI-generated content carries visible, non-removable labels identifying it as artificial, with a three-hour takedown window for high-risk violations such as non-consensual intimate deepfakes and child sexual abuse material — down from the previous 36 hours.

Those rules, issued under the Information Technology Act, 2000, do not explicitly address AI, and legal experts have warned they could face judicial scrutiny. Cyber law experts have argued that a standalone AI law will be needed, since "rules are secondary in nature and cannot exceed the ambit of the parent law." The consultation paper is the on-ramp to that larger legislation: officials have signaled that a comprehensive AI bill, providing a broader framework for regulating AI-generated content, will follow.

Not the same as Modi's global pitch

Separately, on the same day, Prime Minister Narendra Modi used the India Mobile Congress to call for a global framework to combat cyber fraud, deepfakes, and digital crime. Vaishnaw's announcement is the domestic counterpart — the mechanism by which India builds its own AI rulebook, paper by paper, before any global consensus exists.

What it means for the diaspora

For the Indian tech diaspora — engineers, product leaders, and founders building AI products used in India — the consultation is the moment to engage. Whatever emerges will set compliance duties for global platforms operating in India, from labeling requirements to takedown timelines, and startups serving Indian users will need to design for disclosure from day one. The industry-heavy approach Vaishnaw described means the companies doing the most business in India will have the loudest voice in the room — and the largest obligations at the end.

What's next

Watch for the consultation paper's release in the coming weeks, then the feedback window for industry and civil society. The substance of the final rules — how strict labeling and takedown duties become, and how far a future AI bill reaches into criminal liability for deepfake abuse — will be settled in that public comment process.
